gaps.concept: Congenital toxoplasmosis is most severe after early gestational infection, although fetal transmission becomes more likely later in pregnancy.
gaps.why_tested: A stem gives the gestational timing of maternal infection and asks about fetal risk or severity.

gaps.concept: Maternal toxoplasmosis without established fetal infection is treated with spiramycin; confirmed fetal infection uses pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin.
gaps.why_tested: A stem asks which drug regimen reduces transmission or treats an infected fetus.

gaps.concept: Interstitial keratitis completes the late congenital syphilis triad with Hutchinson teeth and sensorineural deafness.
gaps.why_tested: A child has dental abnormalities and hearing loss, and the question asks for another expected finding.

gaps.concept: Congenital syphilis causes long-bone osteochondritis or periostitis, producing painful pseudoparalysis.
gaps.why_tested: A neonate with maternal syphilis does not move an extremity and has abnormal long-bone radiographs.

gaps.concept: Penicillin G is the only reliably effective treatment for fetal syphilis; penicillin-allergic pregnant patients require desensitization.
gaps.why_tested: A penicillin-allergic pregnant patient has syphilis, and the stem asks how to prevent congenital infection.

gaps.concept: A neonatal nontreponemal syphilis titer at least fourfold higher than the maternal titer strongly supports congenital infection.
gaps.why_tested: Maternal and infant RPR titers are provided, and the question asks whether infant seroreactivity reflects infection.

gaps.concept: Maternal rubella infection in the first trimester carries the greatest risk of congenital anomalies.
gaps.why_tested: A pregnant patient develops rubella at a specified gestational age, and the stem asks about fetal risk.

gaps.concept: Congenital CMV may cause petechiae, thrombocytopenia, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly.
gaps.why_tested: A newborn has hearing loss plus a petechial rash or low platelet count, distinguishing CMV from other congenital infections.

gaps.concept: Congenital CMV is confirmed by saliva PCR with urine confirmation within three weeks of birth; infant antibody tests cannot establish it.
gaps.why_tested: A newborn fails hearing screening, and the question asks which test distinguishes congenital from postnatal CMV.

gaps.concept: Symptomatic congenital CMV may be treated with ganciclovir or valganciclovir, which can cause neutropenia.
gaps.why_tested: A symptomatic CMV-infected newborn receives antiviral therapy, and the stem asks for the drug or adverse effect.

gaps.concept: New maternal genital HSV infection near delivery has much greater neonatal transmission risk than recurrent HSV because protective maternal antibodies are absent.
gaps.why_tested: A stem contrasts first-episode and recurrent maternal HSV at delivery.

gaps.concept: Suspected neonatal HSV is evaluated with HSV PCR and treated with intravenous acyclovir, including CNS or disseminated disease.
gaps.why_tested: A newborn develops vesicles, seizures, or sepsis after maternal genital HSV exposure.

gaps.concept: Maternal parvovirus B19 infection may present with slapped-cheek rash, lacy rash, or arthralgia after exposure to an infected child.
gaps.why_tested: A pregnant teacher has rash or joint pain before fetal anemia or hydrops is detected.

gaps.concept: Maternal varicella rash from five days before through two days after delivery risks severe neonatal varicella because protective IgG has not transferred.
gaps.why_tested: A mother develops chickenpox immediately around delivery, and the stem asks why her newborn is at high risk.

gaps.concept: Neonatal listeriosis can produce granulomatosis infantiseptica; Listeria is a motile, intracellular gram-positive rod.
gaps.why_tested: A febrile pregnant patient delivers a septic neonate with disseminated granulomas or characteristic bacterial motility.

gaps.concept: GBS is Streptococcus agalactiae: a beta-hemolytic, CAMP-positive, bacitracin-resistant gram-positive coccus.
gaps.why_tested: A neonatal sepsis isolate is described by culture reactions rather than named directly.

gaps.concept: GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy or a previous infant with invasive GBS disease independently indicates intrapartum prophylaxis.
gaps.why_tested: A laboring patient has no current rectovaginal culture result but has one of these histories.

gaps.concept: Prolonged membrane rupture, prematurity, and intrapartum fever increase early-onset neonatal GBS risk; prophylaxis does not prevent late-onset disease.
gaps.why_tested: A stem asks whether intrapartum antibiotics prevent disease in a newborn presenting weeks after birth.

gaps.concept: Maternal HBeAg indicates high HBV replication and increased perinatal transmission risk.
gaps.why_tested: A pregnant HBsAg-positive patient has additional serology, and the question asks which marker predicts infectivity.

gaps.concept: Perinatally acquired HBV has a much higher risk of chronic infection than adult-acquired HBV.
gaps.why_tested: A stem asks why immediate newborn HBV immunoprophylaxis matters despite an asymptomatic infant.

gaps.concept: Hepatitis C has no vaccine or effective immune-globulin prophylaxis for exposed newborns.
gaps.why_tested: A newborn of an HCV-positive mother is compared with one exposed to HBV.

gaps.concept: Maternal antiretroviral therapy and viral suppression markedly reduce perinatal HIV transmission; HIV-exposed newborns receive antiretroviral prophylaxis.
gaps.why_tested: A pregnant patient has HIV, and the stem asks how maternal viremia or infant prophylaxis affects transmission.

gaps.concept: HIV-exposed infants require HIV nucleic-acid testing; transplacental maternal IgG makes antibody tests unreliable before 18 months.
gaps.why_tested: An infant of a mother with HIV has a positive antibody test, and the stem asks how to establish infection.

gaps.concept: HIV can transmit before birth, during delivery, or through breast milk; maternal viral load strongly affects transmission risk.
gaps.why_tested: A question asks for a transmission route or interprets risk from maternal viral suppression.

gaps.concept: Congenital Zika can cause cortical thinning, subcortical calcifications, and arthrogryposis.
gaps.why_tested: A microcephalic infant has neuroimaging findings that distinguish Zika from periventricular CMV or diffuse toxoplasmosis.

gaps.concept: Zika is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes and can also spread sexually to a pregnant partner.
gaps.why_tested: A pregnant patient has no travel history but has a partner who recently returned from an affected region.

gaps.concept: Erythromycin eye ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia but not chlamydial ophthalmia; established gonococcal infection requires systemic ceftriaxone.
gaps.why_tested: A newborn develops purulent conjunctivitis despite eye prophylaxis, or the stem asks which infection prophylaxis prevents.

gaps.concept: Gonococcal ophthalmia may show intracellular gram-negative diplococci and can cause corneal perforation or blindness.
gaps.why_tested: A rapidly progressive neonatal eye infection includes a conjunctival Gram stain or asks about its complication.

gaps.concept: Neonatal chlamydial infection can cause afebrile pneumonia at one to three months with staccato cough, hyperinflation, and eosinophilia.
gaps.why_tested: An infant with maternal chlamydia exposure develops cough weeks after conjunctivitis.

gaps.concept: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis requires systemic macrolide treatment; topical eye ointment alone is inadequate.
gaps.why_tested: A newborn has chlamydial ophthalmia, and the question asks why topical prophylaxis or treatment is insufficient.

gaps.concept: HPV types 6 and 11 can cause juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis after perinatal exposure.
gaps.why_tested: A child develops recurrent hoarseness or laryngeal papillomas after maternal genital warts.

gaps.concept: Escherichia coli bearing the K1 capsule is another major cause of early neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
gaps.why_tested: A septic neonate has gram-negative rods in blood or cerebrospinal fluid rather than GBS or Listeria.

gaps.concept: Ascending polymicrobial intra-amniotic infection presents with maternal fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, and sometimes foul-smelling amniotic fluid.
gaps.why_tested: A laboring patient has prolonged membrane rupture and signs of infection, and the question asks for the diagnosis.
